entities.summary:
Mahāyāna (‘Great Vehicle’) is a major branch of Buddhism that took shape in India around the turn of the Common Era and spread across Central, East, and Southeast Asia. Emphasising the bodhisattva path, vast cosmologies, and new sūtra literature, it reinterpreted earlier Buddhist goals of individual liberation toward universal compassion and buddhahood for all beings.

Mahāyāna communities developed monasteries, philosophical schools (Madhyamaka, Yogācāra), and devotional cults of buddhas and bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara. Transmission along Silk Road and maritime routes carried these forms into China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, and Vietnam, generating distinctive local canons and arts.

As both doctrine and institutional family, Mahāyāna reshaped Asian religious landscapes for two millennia, remaining one of the principal living streams of Buddhist civilisation.
